Felix uses a 12-inch Dobsonian as his primary scope and prefers red LED headlamps so his night vision stays intact. He always packs a thermos of espresso, a wool blanket, and a little box of sliced Swiss cheese for snack breaks between alignments.

Ethan Rivera spends most mornings in a small garage studio that he converted into a glassblowing shop. He always takes off his shoes at the door and keeps a pair of studio-only clogs by the furnace to avoid tracking outdoor pollen in.

Ethan has severe pollen allergies, specifically to birch and ragweed, so his workspace has a HEPA air purifier running all day and he avoids opening windows during spring. He wears an N95 mask whenever he has to step outside between April and June and schedules no outdoor errands on high-pollen days.

His ritual before a session is making a cup of chamomile tea and checking his kiln temperature twice; he believes the tea calms his hands. Ethan works primarily with soda-lime glass and prefers making goblets with a subtle twist; he has a shelf of roughly 40 signed pieces that friends can borrow for events but not for display with dried flowers.

He refuses to use any floral motifs in commissioned pieces because seeing dried botanicals makes him physically uncomfortable. Ethan keeps a small notebook of color mixes, an old stopwatch for timing anneals, and a ceramic ashtray that he does not use for smoking but keeps as a weight to hold small sketches down.

He also follows a strict rule: no lilies or potpourri in the studio building. On weekends he tutors one apprentice and always insists they bring only sealed water bottles and wear long sleeves to protect from glass shards.
He is allergic enough that he once canceled a gallery opening when the venue insisted on using real garlands.

query: What humidity level should I keep for Felix Andersen's indoor plants?

He refuses to mist plants because of mold concerns and instead uses a humidity dome on delicate seedlings. Watering is an almost-religious Monday ritual: rainwater collected in a barrel, brought to room temperature, and applied to pots every Monday without fail.

He feeds with a compost tea on Thursdays and keeps track of everything in a notebook labeled 'water, feed, measure.' His rule of thumb is simple: if leaf edges brown, lower humidity by five percentage points and wait a week. Felix keeps a small fan running for air circulation but never points it directly at foliage.

query: What's a good time to schedule a lesson with Jonas Weber at the harbor?

Jonas Weber left the podium after a dozen years conducting a city orchestra and now spends mornings at a small harbor teaching sailing, and the rhythm of both professions shows in his lessons. He wears an old navy pea coat on chilly mornings and whistles scale-like patterns when he rigs a boat; crew members joke that he conducts the rigging.

Jonas prefers wind-only sailboats and refuses to take students out on motorboats—he believes learning heel and trim is only honest under sail. He keeps three dinghies named Allegro, Largo and Presto, and he ties an old conducting baton to the mast of his favorite boat as a good-luck charm.

Lessons are usually scheduled after 10:00 AM when wind patterns settle and Jonas has checked the morning reports; he does not radio trainees before noon unless there's an emergency. His teaching method often maps musical concepts to seamanship: tempo to tacking cadence, dynamics to sail trim.

He carries a small silver whistle and a stack of laminated knot cards that show step-by-step sennit and bowline techniques. Jonas refuses to let students skip the basic knot module and insists everyone learns the cleat hitch on day one.
Evenings he still reviews scores for fun, but the harbor is where he prefers to keep his attention now.

Theo Laurent is an architect who has made a habit out of rescuing old factories and turning them into lively, useful places rather than glassy monuments. He keeps a small model-making studio where reclaimed bricks and steel columns are core elements of every mock-up; preserving original brickwork is a favorite constraint.

Theo insists on using reclaimed wood from local demolitions for interior finishes whenever possible and keeps a ledger of trusted salvage yards he visits every month. One rule he enforces on every project is that there must be a community room or public commons in the redeveloped building.
